summary: Offers considerations for deploying Information-Centric Networking (ICN), describing the main deployment configurations, including overlay and underlay approaches, to help the ICN community move toward live deployments.

eli5.summary: A guide for people who want to try a new kind of internet where you ask for things by name, explaining ways to start using it.

subtitle: Roadmap and configurations for deploying Information-Centric Networking as internet infrastructure evolves.

tldr.problem: Information-Centric Networking (ICN) is a mature research approach that names data directly instead of network locations, promising benefits like in-network caching and multicast, but moving from research to real-world deployment requires concrete configurations and migration paths that avoid replacing the entire internet at once.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes five major deployment models (Clean-Slate replacement, Overlay, Underlay, Slice, and Composite) and shows how applications, CDNs, edge networks, and core networks can incrementally adopt ICN. It summarizes trial experiences from multiple ICN projects and identifies protocol standardization gaps that need to be filled.
tldr.outcome: The deployment frameworks enable ICN technologies to be introduced in operational networks at their own pace, from test overlays to production underlays within 5G network slices. Trial experiences across multiple countries and projects demonstrate feasibility.

today: RFC 8763 is an Informational RFC published in April 2020 as the output of the IRTF Information-Centric Networking Research Group. It remains the primary reference for ICN deployment approaches. Ongoing research continues in areas like 5G integration, security standardization, and gateway protocols.

sections.title: Introduction and Context
sections.content:
Information-Centric Networking (ICN) is a network architecture where data objects are named and addressed directly, rather than by the servers and locations that hold them. This shift promises benefits including native multicast (one request serves many receivers), in-network caching (content is cached at intermediate routers), and location-independent delivery (the sender and receiver do not need to know each other's network addresses).

After years of research and experimentation, ICN is reaching maturity. However, complete replacement of the existing internet (a clean-slate approach) is impractical. This RFC addresses the gap by defining concrete deployment configurations and migration paths that allow ICN to be introduced into networks incrementally, working alongside existing IP infrastructure.
sections.eli5: A new way to send data on the internet could be much better. But you cannot replace the whole internet overnight. This document shows how to add it piece by piece.

sections.title: Deployment Configurations
sections.content:
The RFC identifies five major deployment models. Clean-Slate ICN would replace all IP infrastructure with ICN routers—theoretically ideal but practically unrealistic. ICN-as-an-Overlay creates islands of ICN networks (like virtual networks using ICN-over-UDP or HTTP convergence layers) tunneled over existing IP infrastructure. This allows rapid experimentation and testing.

ICN-as-an-Underlay deploys native ICN networks inside specific domains (CDNs, edge IoT networks, mobile cores) and uses protocol gateways to convert between ICN and IP at domain boundaries. This lets applications benefit from native ICN features while appearing as normal IP services to external networks. ICN-as-a-Slice leverages network slicing (SDN and NFV) to allocate dedicated ICN slices within 5G and similar softwarized networks, offering service isolation and independent scaling.

Composite-ICN describes hybrid approaches that do not fit neatly into one category, such as Hybrid ICN which embeds ICN names in IPv6 packets so ICN-aware and IP-only routers can coexist.
sections.eli5: Five ways to add ICN: replace everything (impractical), build test networks on top of IP, build production networks inside specific domains, use network slicing in 5G, or mix approaches.

sections.title: Migration Pathways
sections.content:
For applications, the Underlay approach supports proxy-based message mapping (translating HTTP/TCP/IP to ICN equivalents at domain edges) for existing applications, while Overlay and Slice approaches enable new ICN-native applications that exploit capabilities like multicast and caching directly. A dual-stack middleware can adapt applications dynamically to either protocol stack.

Content Delivery Networks can migrate by placing ICN islands within CDN server farms, letting the ICN infrastructure handle internal content routing and caching while gateways present standard HTTP to the public internet. Edge networks (IoT, mobile access) can adopt Underlay (using application gateways for CoAP-to-ICN translation) or Slice (as dedicated ICN access slices in 5G). Core networks can use Slice to isolate ICN routing within slices of SDN-based optical transport, or Underlay with NAPs (Network Attachment Points) that map HTTP to ICN at ingress and back to HTTP at egress.
sections.eli5: Different parts of the network migrate differently. Apps get adapters. CDNs get internal ICN islands. Phones get ICN slices. Backbone routers keep being IP but run ICN in SDN slices.

sections.title: Trial Experiences and Lessons
sections.content:
Multiple real deployments demonstrate viability. Overlay trials (FP7 PURSUIT, NDN Testbed, ICN2020) deployed 70+ to 100+ node testbeds across continents, running video conferencing and content delivery over tunneled ICN. Peak throughputs reached 70 Mbps per node. Underlay trials (H2020 POINT/RIFE, FLAME, DOCTOR) deployed 40+ nodes in production environments including commercial ISPs and city-scale networks, demonstrating multicast-based video delivery and edge computing scenarios. CableLabs evaluated ICN within CDN server farms for improved in-network caching.

IoT trials (NDN on 6LoWPAN with 60 nodes) showed 60% ROM and 80% RAM footprint reductions versus IP-based IoT stacks. Hybrid ICN trials with 150+ video clients showed good scalability. The key finding: all trials operated at less than 1000 users, and clean-slate replacement was abandoned as unrealistic. Composite approaches showed promise for coexistence.
sections.eli5: Teams have built real networks with ICN. Test networks worked. City networks worked. Even tiny wireless networks worked better than IP. All of them kept IP as backup instead of replacing it.

sections.title: Standardization Gaps and Next Steps
sections.content:
Despite successful trials, three key areas require IETF standardization for interoperable ICN deployments. Application and Service Migration needs standard APIs and communication paradigms so applications can leverage ICN capabilities like named-based requests and multicast, similar to how REST and sockets standardized IP. Content Delivery Network Migration requires standards for naming dynamically generated content (current naming conventions suit static objects but not video streams) and multicast-based content distribution within CDNs.

Edge and Core Network Migration needs standardized protocols for ICN-to-IP gateways, security in ICN domains, and interoperability frameworks. Additionally, mobile network integration (how 5G handles ICN traffic and mobility), virtualization support (NFV/MANO orchestration for ICN), and SDN integration for programmable forwarding are areas needing further work. The RFC recommends these be addressed through IETF standards processes to enable vendor interoperability.
sections.eli5: Networks need three things standardized before ICN can become mainstream: how apps talk to ICN, how content delivery works in ICN, and how ICN routers talk to IP routers reliably.
